scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire research letter (title, methods, results, discussion) concerns lost labor costs associated with Long COVID (LC) using 2022 MEPS data; Lyme disease is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed research letter (JABFM, 2025) that used 2022 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data on US adult full-time workers to estimate the cost of workdays missed due to illness among people with Long COVID (defined as COVID-19 symptoms lasting 3+ months), compared with people who had COVID-19 without Long COVID and people who never had COVID-19. Using a human-capital (wage-based) approach, the authors found that individuals with Long COVID had substantially higher average lost-labor costs than the other two groups, and they extrapolated this to a national population-level estimate of over $12 billion in lost labor costs in 2022. The study covers only wage/workday-loss burden for employed full-time workers; it does not address direct medical costs, non-medical costs, caregiving burden, or people who left the workforce entirely due to Long COVID.

contextual_issues: Direct medical costs of Long COVID care are mentioned only as a general prior-literature topic (citing other studies) and are not measured or modeled in this document.
Direct non-medical costs (e.g., travel, paid help, home modifications) are not addressed at all.
Caregiving time or caregiver burden is not addressed.
Delayed diagnosis, diagnostic uncertainty, and repeated care-seeking are not addressed.
Insurance coverage and access-to-care barriers are not addressed beyond the single paid-sick-leave variable.
Presenteeism (reduced productivity while still working) is not measured; the study captures only absenteeism (missed workdays).
Long-term or lifetime financial consequences beyond the single 2022 calendar year are not addressed.
evidence_gaps: No data on individuals who left the workforce entirely or reduced hours below 35/week because of Long COVID; the study population is restricted to full-time workers (35-100 hrs/week) with available wage/workday data, so total labor-market burden is likely undercounted.
No measurement of direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, or caregiving costs to combine with the lost-labor estimate into a total cost-of-illness figure.
No multi-year data; the analysis is cross-sectional for calendar year 2022 only, so a lifetime or multi-year cost cannot be derived without an added assumption.
No subgroup breakdowns (sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, veteran status, etc.) are reported for any of the cost estimates.

Reliance on self-reported COVID-19/Long COVID history and self-reported missed workdays, which the authors themselves note may lead to under- or overestimation, and lack of a direct measure isolating sick days specifically attributable to Long COVID.
comparison_boundaries: Do not add or average this study's real-world, self-reported, human-capital-based estimate (~$12.8 billion, 2022, US full-time workers only) with the previously published modeling study the authors cite ($1.99-$6.49 billion in employer productivity losses 'as of early 2024') - the document itself states these differ in method (real-world observed missed-workdays vs. a prior modeling approach), population, and measurement time window, and does not adopt the cited figure as its own.

Do not treat the 'total cost' figures in Table 1 as measures of per-person burden: the document explicitly states the Long COVID group's total cost is lowest only because it has the fewest weighted individuals (8,158,551) versus the much larger 'never had COVID-19' (44,156,049) and 'had COVID-19 without Long COVID' (52,575,022) groups; only the mean/median per-individual costs are comparable across groups.

The printed Table 1 total-cost column contains an apparent internal inconsistency/data-entry artifact (the 'Never had COVID-19' and 'Had long COVID' rows show identical total-cost and SE values, which conflicts with the distinct figures given in the Results text: $31,016,098,164 for never-had-COVID-19 vs. $15,863,994,281 for Long COVID). This analysis relies on the values stated in the Results section prose rather than the table's printed total-cost numbers for those two groups.

The population-level estimate ($12,784,168,675.20) is a formula-based national extrapolation (BLS 2022 full-time worker count x study-sample LC prevalence x observed mean-cost difference) and is a structurally different quantity from the MEPS survey-weighted group totals in Table 1; the two should be treated as distinct measurement approaches, not interchangeable or additive figures.

All dollar figures in this document are 2022 price-year, human-capital/lost-wage estimates from a single MEPS cross-section; they should not be pooled with cost estimates using a different perspective (e.g., employer cost, health-plan payer cost, or patient out-of-pocket cost) without separately identifying the perspective and price year.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The population-level lost labor cost associated with Long COVID in 2022 ($12,784,168,675.20) and the group-level total/mean lost labor cost figures in Table 1/Table 2 are all presented as single pooled national or group-level figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status, and the document does not state that subgroup variation was checked and found negligible.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document states that there are currently no effective treatments for Long COVID, framing vaccination as 'the best available strategy' for prevention and calling to 'accelerate research into effective therapies' - indicating no established treatment pathway currently exists for the condition.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section, p.942: 'In the absence of effective treatments, these consequences underscore the need to prioritize prevention through vaccination — the best available strategy to reduce the risk of LC — and accelerate research into effective therapies.'

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire research letter (title, methods, results, discussion) concerns lost labor costs associated with Long COVID (LC) using 2022 MEPS data; Lyme disease is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed research letter (JABFM, 2025) that used 2022 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data on US adult full-time workers to estimate the cost of workdays missed due to illness among people with Long COVID (defined as COVID-19 symptoms lasting 3+ months), compared with people who had COVID-19 without Long COVID and people who never had COVID-19. Using a human-capital (wage-based) approach, the authors found that individuals with Long COVID had substantially higher average lost-labor costs than the other two groups, and they extrapolated this to a national population-level estimate of over $12 billion in lost labor costs in 2022. The study covers only wage/workday-loss burden for employed full-time workers; it does not address direct medical costs, non-medical costs, caregiving burden, or people who left the workforce entirely due to Long COVID.

contextual_issues: Direct medical costs of Long COVID care are mentioned only as a general prior-literature topic (citing other studies) and are not measured or modeled in this document.
Direct non-medical costs (e.g., travel, paid help, home modifications) are not addressed at all.
Caregiving time or caregiver burden is not addressed.
Delayed diagnosis, diagnostic uncertainty, and repeated care-seeking are not addressed.
Insurance coverage and access-to-care barriers are not addressed beyond the single paid-sick-leave variable.
Presenteeism (reduced productivity while still working) is not measured; the study captures only absenteeism (missed workdays).
Long-term or lifetime financial consequences beyond the single 2022 calendar year are not addressed.
evidence_gaps: No data on individuals who left the workforce entirely or reduced hours below 35/week because of Long COVID; the study population is restricted to full-time workers (35-100 hrs/week) with available wage/workday data, so total labor-market burden is likely undercounted.
No measurement of direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, or caregiving costs to combine with the lost-labor estimate into a total cost-of-illness figure.
No multi-year data; the analysis is cross-sectional for calendar year 2022 only, so a lifetime or multi-year cost cannot be derived without an added assumption.
No subgroup breakdowns (sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, veteran status, etc.) are reported for any of the cost estimates.

Reliance on self-reported COVID-19/Long COVID history and self-reported missed workdays, which the authors themselves note may lead to under- or overestimation, and lack of a direct measure isolating sick days specifically attributable to Long COVID.
comparison_boundaries: Do not add or average this study's real-world, self-reported, human-capital-based estimate (~$12.8 billion, 2022, US full-time workers only) with the previously published modeling study the authors cite ($1.99-$6.49 billion in employer productivity losses 'as of early 2024') - the document itself states these differ in method (real-world observed missed-workdays vs. a prior modeling approach), population, and measurement time window, and does not adopt the cited figure as its own.

Do not treat the 'total cost' figures in Table 1 as measures of per-person burden: the document explicitly states the Long COVID group's total cost is lowest only because it has the fewest weighted individuals (8,158,551) versus the much larger 'never had COVID-19' (44,156,049) and 'had COVID-19 without Long COVID' (52,575,022) groups; only the mean/median per-individual costs are comparable across groups.

The printed Table 1 total-cost column contains an apparent internal inconsistency/data-entry artifact (the 'Never had COVID-19' and 'Had long COVID' rows show identical total-cost and SE values, which conflicts with the distinct figures given in the Results text: $31,016,098,164 for never-had-COVID-19 vs. $15,863,994,281 for Long COVID). This analysis relies on the values stated in the Results section prose rather than the table's printed total-cost numbers for those two groups.

The population-level estimate ($12,784,168,675.20) is a formula-based national extrapolation (BLS 2022 full-time worker count x study-sample LC prevalence x observed mean-cost difference) and is a structurally different quantity from the MEPS survey-weighted group totals in Table 1; the two should be treated as distinct measurement approaches, not interchangeable or additive figures.

All dollar figures in this document are 2022 price-year, human-capital/lost-wage estimates from a single MEPS cross-section; they should not be pooled with cost estimates using a different perspective (e.g., employer cost, health-plan payer cost, or patient out-of-pocket cost) without separately identifying the perspective and price year.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The population-level lost labor cost associated with Long COVID in 2022 ($12,784,168,675.20) and the group-level total/mean lost labor cost figures in Table 1/Table 2 are all presented as single pooled national or group-level figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status, and the document does not state that subgroup variation was checked and found negligible.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document states that there are currently no effective treatments for Long COVID, framing vaccination as 'the best available strategy' for prevention and calling to 'accelerate research into effective therapies' - indicating no established treatment pathway currently exists for the condition.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section, p.942: 'In the absence of effective treatments, these consequences underscore the need to prioritize prevention through vaccination — the best available strategy to reduce the risk of LC — and accelerate research into effective therapies.'

spec.title: Long COVID Lost Labor Cost Simulator (2022 MEPS, US Full-Time Workers)
spec.boundary: This simulation covers only self-reported, wage-based lost-workday ('lost labor') costs for US adults still working full-time in 2022, as measured in a single MEPS survey cross-section. It does not include direct medical costs, non-medical costs, caregiving burden, presenteeism (reduced productivity while still working), or anyone who reduced hours or left the workforce entirely because of Long COVID. The national projection is a formula-based extrapolation, not a directly measured total, and is a structurally different quantity from the survey-weighted group totals the document also reports.

takeaway.patient: In this 2022 US national survey of full-time workers, people with Long COVID (COVID-19 symptoms lasting 3 or more months) lost an average of about $1,944 in wages from missed workdays over the year, compared with about $702 for people who never had COVID-19 and about $1,466 for people who had COVID-19 but did not develop Long COVID. The gap versus never having had COVID-19 was large and very statistically reliable; the smaller gap versus COVID-19 without Long COVID was also statistically significant, but only just barely. Paid sick leave access was similar across all three groups and was not statistically linked to having Long COVID.
takeaway.care: Among full-time workers in the 2022 MEPS national survey, patients with Long COVID had notably higher average lost-workday costs (about $1,944) than patients who never had COVID-19 (about $702) and patients who had COVID-19 without Long COVID (about $1,466). The comparison with never-had-COVID-19 patients was strongly statistically significant; the comparison with COVID-without-Long-COVID patients was significant but only marginally so. Paid sick leave prevalence did not differ significantly by Long COVID status, suggesting absenteeism-related cost differences are not simply explained by differential leave access.
takeaway.policy: Using 2022 MEPS data on US full-time workers, the study reports average per-person lost-labor costs of about $1,944 for workers with Long COVID versus about $702 for those who never had COVID-19 (a highly significant ~$1,242 gap) and about $1,466 for those who had COVID-19 without Long COVID (a smaller, only marginally significant ~$479 gap). Scaling the stronger per-person gap by national full-time workforce size and Long COVID prevalence, the authors project a 2022 national lost-labor-cost burden exceeding $12.8 billion. This is a formula-based projection, not a measured national total, and covers only wage/workday losses among people still working full-time.

patient: If you have Long COVID and have missed work, this data suggests your wage loss from missed workdays may be substantially higher than typical; it may help to raise this with your employer's HR or benefits team when discussing leave or accommodation options.

Ask about your workplace's paid sick leave policy specifically - the study found paid leave access was similar regardless of Long COVID status, so leave policy itself may not be the main source of any gap you're experiencing.

This study only counted missed full workdays for people still working full-time; if you reduced your hours or stopped working because of Long COVID, your own financial impact may be larger than these figures capture, which may be worth noting when talking with advocates or support groups.
care: This finding may be worth checking against your own absence-management or return-to-work workflows for patients reporting persistent post-COVID symptoms, since this group showed meaningfully higher missed-workday costs than the comparison groups.

Since the document notes no effective treatments currently exist for Long COVID, teams coordinating with occupational health or employer benefits staff may want to flag that accommodation and work-modification pathways, rather than treatment, are the main lever currently available for these patients.

Consider whether intake or follow-up processes capture missed-workday counts in a structured way, since the study relied on self-report and could not isolate days attributable specifically to Long COVID versus other causes.
policy: Use the per-person lost-labor-cost gap and the national projection as one component (labor costs only) when scoping the scale of Long COVID's 2022 economic impact; do not add it to medical-cost or caregiving-cost estimates from other sources without separately labeling each component's perspective and price year.

Treat the national figure as a formula-based projection (per-person cost gap x prevalence x workforce size), not a directly measured total; the document's own survey-weighted group totals are a structurally different quantity and should not be combined with it.

Because these pooled estimates have not been checked for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, consider reviewing disaggregated analysis (e.g., via MEPS, NHIS, or BRFSS) before using this figure to target subgroup-specific interventions.

Given the document's note that no effective treatments currently exist for Long COVID, this labor-cost burden may be relevant context for weighing research-funding or prevention (e.g., vaccination) investment priorities, kept separate from the cost-measurement question itself.

## Source
This simulator is built from a 2025 JABFM peer-reviewed research letter estimating 2022 lost-labor costs associated with Long COVID using Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data on US full-time workers (35-100 hrs/week), via a human-capital (wage x hours x missed days) approach.

## Inputs and outputs
Three inputs are the document's own observed mean per-person lost-labor costs (2022 USD) for workers with Long COVID, workers who never had COVID-19, and workers who had COVID-19 without Long COVID. spec.title: Long COVID Lost Labor Cost Simulator (2022 MEPS, US Full-Time Workers)
spec.boundary: This simulation covers only self-reported, wage-based lost-workday ('lost labor') costs for US adults still working full-time in 2022, as measured in a single MEPS survey cross-section. It does not include direct medical costs, non-medical costs, caregiving burden, presenteeism (reduced productivity while still working), or anyone who reduced hours or left the workforce entirely because of Long COVID. The national projection is a formula-based extrapolation, not a directly measured total, and is a structurally different quantity from the survey-weighted group totals the document also reports.

takeaway.patient: In this 2022 US national survey of full-time workers, people with Long COVID (COVID-19 symptoms lasting 3 or more months) lost an average of about $1,944 in wages from missed workdays over the year, compared with about $702 for people who never had COVID-19 and about $1,466 for people who had COVID-19 but did not develop Long COVID. The gap versus never having had COVID-19 was large and very statistically reliable; the smaller gap versus COVID-19 without Long COVID was also statistically significant, but only just barely. Paid sick leave access was similar across all three groups and was not statistically linked to having Long COVID.
takeaway.care: Among full-time workers in the 2022 MEPS national survey, patients with Long COVID had notably higher average lost-workday costs (about $1,944) than patients who never had COVID-19 (about $702) and patients who had COVID-19 without Long COVID (about $1,466). The comparison with never-had-COVID-19 patients was strongly statistically significant; the comparison with COVID-without-Long-COVID patients was significant but only marginally so. Paid sick leave prevalence did not differ significantly by Long COVID status, suggesting absenteeism-related cost differences are not simply explained by differential leave access.
takeaway.policy: Using 2022 MEPS data on US full-time workers, the study reports average per-person lost-labor costs of about $1,944 for workers with Long COVID versus about $702 for those who never had COVID-19 (a highly significant ~$1,242 gap) and about $1,466 for those who had COVID-19 without Long COVID (a smaller, only marginally significant ~$479 gap). Scaling the stronger per-person gap by national full-time workforce size and Long COVID prevalence, the authors project a 2022 national lost-labor-cost burden exceeding $12.8 billion. This is a formula-based projection, not a measured national total, and covers only wage/workday losses among people still working full-time.

patient: If you have Long COVID and have missed work, this data suggests your wage loss from missed workdays may be substantially higher than typical; it may help to raise this with your employer's HR or benefits team when discussing leave or accommodation options.

Ask about your workplace's paid sick leave policy specifically - the study found paid leave access was similar regardless of Long COVID status, so leave policy itself may not be the main source of any gap you're experiencing.

This study only counted missed full workdays for people still working full-time; if you reduced your hours or stopped working because of Long COVID, your own financial impact may be larger than these figures capture, which may be worth noting when talking with advocates or support groups.
care: This finding may be worth checking against your own absence-management or return-to-work workflows for patients reporting persistent post-COVID symptoms, since this group showed meaningfully higher missed-workday costs than the comparison groups.

Since the document notes no effective treatments currently exist for Long COVID, teams coordinating with occupational health or employer benefits staff may want to flag that accommodation and work-modification pathways, rather than treatment, are the main lever currently available for these patients.

Consider whether intake or follow-up processes capture missed-workday counts in a structured way, since the study relied on self-report and could not isolate days attributable specifically to Long COVID versus other causes.
policy: Use the per-person lost-labor-cost gap and the national projection as one component (labor costs only) when scoping the scale of Long COVID's 2022 economic impact; do not add it to medical-cost or caregiving-cost estimates from other sources without separately labeling each component's perspective and price year.

Treat the national figure as a formula-based projection (per-person cost gap x prevalence x workforce size), not a directly measured total; the document's own survey-weighted group totals are a structurally different quantity and should not be combined with it.

Because these pooled estimates have not been checked for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, consider reviewing disaggregated analysis (e.g., via MEPS, NHIS, or BRFSS) before using this figure to target subgroup-specific interventions.

Given the document's note that no effective treatments currently exist for Long COVID, this labor-cost burden may be relevant context for weighing research-funding or prevention (e.g., vaccination) investment priorities, kept separate from the cost-measurement question itself.
